config.title: Driving Licence in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: When the six-month clock starts, which countries and US states convert without a test, what Berlin charges, how far behind the licence desk is right now, and the difference between a 10 euro fine and a criminal record.

items.q: How long can I drive in Berlin on a foreign licence?
items.a: If it was issued outside the EU and the EEA, six months from the day you registered an address in Germany. That is section 29 of the Fahrerlaubnis-Verordnung, and the clock runs from the Anmeldung, not from your arrival or from the date on your visa. You can apply to the authority to extend it by up to six more months, but only if you can make it credible that you will not be resident in Germany for longer than twelve months in total. An EU or EEA licence has no six-month rule and stays valid until the date printed on it.

items.q: Do I have to take a driving test to convert my licence in Berlin?
items.a: It depends entirely on where the licence was issued. Anlage 11 of the Fahrerlaubnis-Verordnung names the states whose licences convert with no test, and it lists the United States state by state, Canada province by province and Australia state by state. Twenty-six countries and territories convert test-free, including Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel, Singapore, South Africa, New Zealand, Serbia, Ukraine and Taiwan, along with all of Canada, all of Australia and 28 US jurisdictions. Eleven US entries need the German theory exam. Anything not named on the list means both the theory test and the practical drive.

items.q: Which US states are not on the German Anlage 11 list?
items.a: Thirteen: Alaska, California, Georgia, Hawaii, Maine, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Rhode Island and Vermont. A licence from one of those is treated like any other third-country licence, so the holder sits the German theory exam and the practical drive, needs a first aid course and an eyesight test, and pays 45.10 euro. A licence from Michigan or Texas, meanwhile, converts with no test at all.

items.q: What does it cost to convert a driving licence in Berlin?
items.a: The Berlin fee table in force since 1 January 2025 charges 37.50 euro to convert an EU or EEA licence, 37.50 euro to convert an Anlage 11 licence without a test, and 45.10 euro when a test is involved or the licence comes from a third country. Swapping an old German licence for the current card is 26.50 euro and an international driving permit is 15 euro. Express production adds 7.70 euro. On top of the fee, only the third-country lane needs a first aid course, which runs from about 35 euro at a small Berlin provider to 70 euro at the DRK, plus an eyesight test, and any licence written in neither German nor English needs a certified translation.

items.q: How long does the Berlin licence desk take?
items.a: The Landesamt fuer Buerger- und Ordnungsangelegenheiten publishes the application date it is currently working through. On 15 September 2026 the board showed third-country conversions from 31 July, EU conversions from 27 July, Anlage 11 conversions from 20 August, and German card swaps from 27 August. That is between two and a half and seven weeks of processing, and it only starts once every document and fee has reached the authority. It is time after your appointment, so subtract it from your own deadline rather than adding it.

items.q: Where do I apply in Berlin?
items.a: Not at the licence authority itself. The third-country and Anlage 11 conversion can be filed at 57 Berlin locations and the old-licence card swap at 72, and almost all of them are ordinary Buergeraemter. You need a main residence in Berlin, you have to appear in person, and you bring a paper biometric photo because nothing is printed on site. Your foreign licence has to still be valid on the day you apply, and an international driving permit is never converted, only the national licence behind it.

items.q: When does my old German licence expire?
items.a: Every German licence issued before 19 January 2013 has to be swapped for the current EU card in waves. The paper waves ran by birth year and all have closed except the one for holders born before 1953, which runs to 19 January 2033. The card waves run by the year at field 4a: 1999 to 2001 closed on 19 January 2026, 2002 to 2004 closes on 19 January 2027, 2005 to 2007 on 19 January 2028, then 2008 through 2012 and the first days of January 2013 one year at a time to 19 January 2033. The new card must already be in your hand on the deadline, not merely applied for.

items.q: What happens if I drive after the deadline?
items.a: The two cases are not remotely the same. An un-swapped old German licence is a document problem: the entitlement itself never expires, so driving a car or motorbike on it is an Ordnungswidrigkeit worth a 10 euro warning fine. The real cost there is abroad, where a hire desk can refuse a document its system reads as expired. Driving after your six months on a non-EU licence have run out is Fahren ohne Fahrerlaubnis under section 21 of the Strassenverkehrsgesetz: up to a year of imprisonment or a fine, six months or up to 180 daily rates if it was merely negligent, confiscation of the vehicle in listed cases, and an insurer who can come after you for the damage it paid out.
